cover: This talk is about typing promise resolution in the SKJS verifier: contracts for native promises, a sound generic Awaited type, and where TypeScript's own Awaited is unsound. The generic part is partly supported, and the forms it does not yet cover are recorded as gaps.
outline: There are five parts. First, the problem: generic forwarding has no sound type. Second, TypeScript's Awaited, and why it is unsound. Third, contracts for native promises. Fourth, generic Awaited of T, through qualified binders. And fifth, the results: target programs, the census of the corpus, and the limits that remain.
problem: Here is the problem. The function wrap takes a value x of any type T and returns it from an async function, promising a Promise of Awaited of T. On the base branch, the verifier cannot check this. Its two trusted contracts, for await and for async return, only allow primitives on the non-promise side. But T may be a promise or an object, and no type says what x becomes once a promise resolves with it. So wrap is refused.
types: Five definitions. Prim is the primitives, and Obj everything else. A thenable is an object with a callable then. Resolution fulfills a promise directly with a primitive or a non-thenable, and calls a thenable's then. Promise of B is a native promise whose fulfillment values lie in B. And N is the set of values that can never have a callable then.
awaited: TypeScript already has an answer: the Awaited type. It is a conditional type. Null and undefined map to themselves. An object type that declares a then method is unwrapped recursively through the first parameter of its callback. Everything else, including object types with no declared then, maps to itself. Crucially, all of this is decided from the declared type.
unsound: That is unsound, because object types are open. In the first example, a record with a hidden then method is passed as a plain record of type n number. TypeScript says the awaited value is that record, but Node delivers the string hi. In the second example, an object acquires a then method after a promise has fulfilled with it. Awaiting the promise gives the object, and awaiting the object again gives 42, while TypeScript claims both are the record type. So resolution is not idempotent.
twice: There is a second problem, which any design must face: resolution can happen twice. Here a promise fulfills with an object, and the object acquires a then method afterwards. Await, Promise dot resolve, and Promise dot all read the fulfillment value once, and give back the original object. But an async return, then, catch, finally, and the Promise constructor all resolve a fresh promise with that value, and so they call the new then, and produce 42. So observing a fulfillment value is safe at any payload, while resolving it again is safe only if the payload stays non-thenable.
native: That leads to the native promise contracts. A Promise of B is a native promise with stable standard behaviour. Await observes, so it admits a promise of any payload T, and a value in N, the stable non-thenables, at its own type. Async return, Promise dot resolve of a plain value, catch and finally resolve again, so they require their payloads to lie in N. Promise dot resolve of an existing native promise returns that promise itself, so it admits any payload. These are the concrete instances of qualified intrinsics we will see in a moment.
qualified: Now the generic case. When a signature mentions Awaited of T, that mention implies a bound on T, as if it had been written there. Bounds are read off the signature, never off the body. There are two such bounds, and a program can also write them explicitly. T extends Awaitable gives T an observed type, what await yields. That is all await needs. T extends Resolvable also gives T a result type, what a fresh resolution yields, which is never thenable. Async return needs it, and Awaited of T is T's result type. So wrap reads as: for every resolvable T, a function from T to a promise of T's result. And log, which only awaits its argument, needs T to be awaitable. The intrinsics follow the same pattern: await takes any awaitable X and yields its observed type, and async return takes a resolvable X and yields a promise of its result. Neither is a subtype bound: the values of T are unconstrained, and each call supplies the classification of its type argument. There is one other implied bound: a promise argument of an imported or library signature implies that T is a stable non-thenable.
rules: So who fixes the observed and result types? Three rules classify a type argument. A stable type is its own observed and result type. A native promise of A is observed as A, whatever A is, and its result is A's result. And a union is classified arm by arm. A lemma states exactness: on a stable type, the observed type and the result are the type itself. With only these three rules, a stable type has exactly one observation and one result. Who decides the classification? The OCaml producer proposes types only. Lean's proof search finds the classification of each call's type argument, and the Lean checker checks it. Inside a body the two types stay abstract: the result is never thenable, and the observed type resolves to the result.
compare: Comparing TypeScript's Awaited with the result type. On primitives they agree. On a promise of number, and on a promise of a promise of number, both give number. On a union of a number and a promise of a readonly string array, both give number or readonly string array. On an open record, Awaited gives the record, which is unsound, while there is no classification, so the program is refused. The same holds for PromiseLike. In short, the result type agrees with Awaited wherever the result stays non-thenable, and refuses where Awaited is unsound.
targets: Here is where the target programs stand. Parameters and mutable cells of Awaited of T verify. The generic wrap with return await verifies, and so do its calls at a number, an array, native promises and unions. Settle, with T extends Resolvable, verifies. Log, with T extends Awaitable, verifies even at a promise of an open record, since it only observes. The number-bounded function back verifies by exactness: Awaited of T is T itself. Calling wrap at an open record, the erasure to Promise of unknown, and forwarding a promise of a record, the 42 case, are all refused. Overall, all 903 pipeline cases meet their expected outcome, and five generic promise cases are recorded as gaps.
census: On the SKJS corpus, SKJS accepts 2674 units. The verifier verified 2466 of them on the thirtieth of September, and 2467 on the ninth of October. No unit moved because of this branch: rerunning each file that moved, at the branch's base, gives the same outcome. Of the six promise units, the one that awaits an array verifies, since an array is a stable value. The two that await a PromiseLike, and the two that return a fresh object from an async function, are refused on principle, because JavaScript would adopt a then method the type does not describe. The last one is a gap: the keys of a Promise type include a unique symbol.
limits: Finally, the limits that remain. Then, catch and finally keep their contracts bounded by the stable non-thenables. Thenable adoption is refused on principle. A bound that names another type parameter gets no stable-bound shortcut, so Awaited of T stays apart from T. Higher-order uses need generic function types, which are outside the fragment. Further rules would extend coverage: the values a Promise executor resolves, a second reaction on an already-settled promise, thenables that only resolve to themselves, and promises that can never fulfill. And two gaps are already listed: an explicit catch of string, and source copies of promises. Thank you.
